title: Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss Syndrome) - New Diagnosis
scenario: David Chen, a 48-year-old telecommunications engineer from Bankstown, NSW, presents to the respiratory clinic with a 3-month history of worsening asthma, persistent sinusitis, and new-onset peripheral neuropathy. He reports recent weight loss of 8 kg, night sweats, and a purpuric rash on his lower limbs. His wife accompanies him and mentions he has been using his salbutamol inhaler 6-8 times daily. Past medical history includes adult-onset asthma diagnosed 2 years ago and allergic rhinitis. He takes Symbicort Turbuhaler 200/6 two puffs BD and salbutamol PRN. Blood tests show eosinophilia (4.2 x 10^9/L) and elevated IgE (890 IU/mL). Chest X-ray reveals patchy bilateral infiltrates.

patient_demographics.name: David Chen
patient_demographics.cultural_background: Chinese-Australian, migrated from Hong Kong 20 years ago

physical_examination.general_appearance: Alert, appears unwell, using accessory muscles of respiration
physical_examination.hands: No clubbing, multiple splinter haemorrhages, palmar erythema
physical_examination.cardiovascular: JVP 3 cm, regular rhythm, no murmurs, peripheral pulses intact but diminished dorsalis pedis bilaterally
physical_examination.respiratory: Bilateral expiratory wheeze throughout all lung fields, reduced air entry at both bases, no crackles
physical_examination.abdomen: Soft, mild hepatomegaly 2 cm below costal margin, no splenomegaly, no masses
physical_examination.neurological: Decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick in stocking distribution bilaterally, absent ankle reflexes, power 4/5 in dorsiflexion bilaterally
physical_examination.skin: Palpable purpura on both shins and dorsal feet, no necrosis, livedo reticularis on thighs
physical_examination.ENT: Bilateral nasal polyps visible, maxillary sinus tenderness, no oral ulcers

blood_tests.FBC: Hb 118 g/L, WCC 18.2 x 10^9/L, neutrophils 10.1 x 10^9/L, eosinophils 4.2 x 10^9/L, platelets 486 x 10^9/L
blood_tests.biochemistry: Na 138 mmol/L, K 4.1 mmol/L, Cr 126 μmol/L (baseline 78), eGFR 58 mL/min/1.73m², ALT 68 U/L, AST 52 U/L
blood_tests.immunology: ANCA positive (p-ANCA pattern), anti-MPO 86 U/mL (normal <5), IgE 890 IU/mL, RF negative, anti-CCP negative

imaging.chest_xray: Bilateral patchy infiltrates in mid and lower zones, no pleural effusion, normal heart size
imaging.hrct_chest: Ground-glass opacities, septal thickening, small bilateral pleural effusions, mediastinal lymphadenopathy

other.ecg: Sinus tachycardia, no ST changes, normal QRS complexes
other.spirometry: FEV1 1.8L (48% predicted), FVC 3.2L (68% predicted), FEV1/FVC 56%, minimal bronchodilator response

immediate: Urgent respiratory review and admission
High-flow oxygen therapy via nasal prongs 4-6 L/min to maintain SpO2 >94%
Prednisolone 60 mg oral daily (PBS code 2089W)
Continue Symbicort Turbuhaler 200/6 two puffs BD (PBS code 8735G)
Salbutamol 5 mg nebulised QID (PBS code 1819D)
Cardiac monitoring for myocarditis
Urgent rheumatology and neurology consults
investigations: Nerve conduction studies for mononeuritis multiplex
Cardiac MRI to assess for myocardial involvement
Skin biopsy of purpuric lesions for vasculitis confirmation
24-hour urine protein and microscopy for casts
Serum tryptase level
Vitamin B12 and folate levels
definitive: Cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg/day oral (PBS code 2156Q) after fertility counselling
Continue high-dose prednisolone with slow taper over 12 months
Prophylactic cotrimoxazole 160/800 mg daily (PBS code 3150M) for PCP prophylaxis
Calcium carbonate 600 mg BD and vitamin D 1000 IU daily for bone protection
Consider rituximab 1000 mg IV (PBS code 10371T) if cyclophosphamide contraindicated
Mepolizumab 100 mg SC monthly (PBS code 11452Y) for maintenance if meets criteria
monitoring: Weekly FBC for first month then monthly (monitor for cyclophosphamide toxicity)
Annual DEXA scan while on steroids

communication_tasks: Explain EGPA diagnosis using patient-friendly language
Discuss the chronic nature and need for immunosuppression
Address fertility concerns with cyclophosphamide therapy
Explain infection risk with immunosuppression
Provide Vasculitis Australia support group information
Discuss driving restrictions with peripheral neuropathy
Arrange family meeting to discuss treatment plan

scoring_criteria.criterion: Correctly identifies EGPA based on asthma, eosinophilia, and systemic features
Recognises multi-organ involvement (lungs, nerves, heart, kidneys, skin)
Orders appropriate ANCA testing and interprets p-ANCA/anti-MPO positivity
Initiates high-dose corticosteroids promptly
Appropriately prescribes cyclophosphamide with fertility counselling
Implements PCP prophylaxis with cotrimoxazole
Arranges appropriate specialist consultations (rheumatology, neurology)
Documents Five Factor Score for prognosis
Explains diagnosis and treatment risks clearly to patient
Addresses cultural considerations and uses professional interpreter if needed
Plans appropriate monitoring for treatment toxicity
Provides patient education materials and support group referral

key_learning_points: EGPA presents with asthma, eosinophilia, and vasculitis affecting multiple organs
P-ANCA/anti-MPO positivity supports diagnosis but is not always present
Five Factor Score predicts prognosis (cardiac, GI, renal, CNS involvement, proteinuria >1g/day)
Treatment requires high-dose steroids plus cyclophosphamide or rituximab
PCP prophylaxis essential with combined immunosuppression
Mepolizumab (anti-IL5) available on PBS for maintenance therapy in eligible patients
red_flags: Cardiac involvement (elevated troponin) - risk of sudden death
GI involvement with bleeding or perforation risk
Severe asthma not responding to standard treatment

title: Accelerated Silicosis - Stonemason with Occupational Lung Disease
scenario: Marco Rossi, a 34-year-old stonemason from Wetherill Park, NSW, presents to the respiratory outpatient clinic with 6 months of progressive dyspnoea and dry cough. He has worked cutting and installing engineered stone benchtops for 8 years, often dry-cutting without adequate respiratory protection. His employer recently arranged screening after another worker was diagnosed with silicosis. He reports significant breathlessness climbing one flight of stairs and has lost 5 kg. He has never smoked and has no other medical history. His wife is 7 months pregnant with their second child, and he is concerned about his ability to work and provide for his family. Chest X-ray shows bilateral upper lobe nodular opacities.

vital_signs.oxygen_saturation: 93% on room air, 88% post 6-minute walk test

physical_examination.general_appearance: Fit-looking young man, mildly tachypnoeic at rest, no distress
physical_examination.hands: No clubbing, stone dust under fingernails, calloused palms
physical_examination.cardiovascular: JVP not elevated, dual heart sounds, no murmurs, no peripheral oedema
physical_examination.respiratory: Symmetrical chest expansion reduced bilaterally, fine inspiratory crackles in upper zones bilaterally, no wheeze
physical_examination.musculoskeletal: Well-developed musculature, no joint swelling or deformity
physical_examination.skin: Multiple minor scars on hands and forearms from work injuries

blood_tests.FBC: Hb 148 g/L, WCC 7.8 x 10^9/L, platelets 286 x 10^9/L
blood_tests.biochemistry: Na 140 mmol/L, K 4.2 mmol/L, Cr 76 μmol/L, eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73m²
blood_tests.LFT: Normal - ALT 28 U/L, AST 31 U/L, ALP 78 U/L, GGT 42 U/L
blood_tests.autoimmune: ANA negative, RF negative, anti-CCP negative

imaging.chest_xray: Bilateral upper lobe predominant nodular opacities, hilar lymphadenopathy, no pleural disease
imaging.hrct_chest: Multiple centrilobular and perilymphatic nodules predominantly in upper lobes, bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy with eggshell calcification, early progressive massive fibrosis in right upper lobe, ground-glass opacities, no honeycombing

respiratory_function.spirometry: FEV1 2.4L (58% predicted), FVC 3.1L (61% predicted), FEV1/FVC 77%, no significant bronchodilator response
respiratory_function.abg_room_air: pH 7.42, PaO2 72 mmHg, PaCO2 36 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L, SaO2 93%

expected_diagnoses.primary: Accelerated silicosis with early progressive massive fibrosis

immediate: Immediate cessation of silica dust exposure - medical certificate for work cessation
Supplemental oxygen therapy PRN to maintain SpO2 >90%
Salbutamol MDI 100 mcg 2 puffs PRN for symptom relief (PBS code 1703W)
Influenza and pneumococcal vaccination
Notify SafeWork NSW for workplace investigation
investigations: Tuberculosis screening - QuantiFERON Gold, sputum AFB and culture
Bronchoscopy with BAL for cell differential and mineralogical analysis
Echocardiogram to assess for pulmonary hypertension
Right heart catheterisation if echo suggests PH
Serum ACE level to exclude sarcoidosis
Consider lung biopsy if diagnosis uncertain
definitive: Lung transplant assessment referral to St Vincent's Hospital Sydney
Pulmonary rehabilitation program enrollment
Nintedanib 150 mg BD (PBS code 11200T) if progressive fibrosis confirmed
Consider corticosteroids only if significant inflammatory component
Home oxygen therapy assessment and prescription if indicated
Sildenafil 20 mg TDS (PBS code 9376K) if pulmonary hypertension confirmed
compensation: icare NSW workers' compensation claim submission
Dust Diseases Board assessment and registration
Legal advice regarding common law damages
Income protection and TPD insurance review
Centrelink Disability Support Pension assessment if unable to work
monitoring: Mental health screening for adjustment disorder
Occupational therapy for work capacity assessment

communication_tasks: Explain silicosis diagnosis and poor prognosis sensitively
Discuss irreversible nature and progressive course
Address work cessation and financial concerns
Explain workers' compensation process
Discuss lung transplant as potential future option
Involve wife in discussions about prognosis and planning
Provide Lung Foundation Australia silicosis resources
Refer to social work for financial counselling

scoring_criteria.criterion: Recognises accelerated silicosis from occupational history and imaging
Immediately removes patient from ongoing exposure
Appropriately notifies SafeWork NSW for workplace investigation
Initiates workers' compensation and Dust Diseases Board processes
Screens for tuberculosis given increased risk with silicosis
Refers early for lung transplant assessment
Prescribes antifibrotic therapy (nintedanib) appropriately
Addresses psychosocial impact and financial concerns
Provides appropriate patient education and support resources
Documents comprehensive occupational exposure history
Arranges appropriate multidisciplinary team involvement

key_learning_points: Engineered stone contains up to 95% crystalline silica - higher risk than natural stone
Accelerated silicosis can develop within 10 years of high-intensity exposure
Early referral for lung transplant assessment crucial given young age
Workers' compensation and Dust Diseases Board provide financial support
SafeWork NSW notification mandatory for workplace investigation
Nintedanib may slow progression of fibrosis in selected cases
Screen for TB as silicosis increases susceptibility 3-fold
red_flags: Rapid decline in lung function over 3-6 months
Signs of pulmonary hypertension or cor pulmonale
Severe hypoxaemia requiring continuous oxygen therapy

title: Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis (Farmer's Lung) - Acute Presentation
scenario: Jennifer Walsh, a 42-year-old dairy farmer from Cobargo, NSW, presents to the emergency department with acute onset of fever, chills, and severe dyspnoea 6 hours after feeding mouldy hay to cattle. She describes similar but milder episodes over the past 3 months, always occurring after working in the hay shed. Symptoms typically improve when she spends time away from the farm. She keeps 120 dairy cows and has recently been using last season's hay due to drought conditions. She has never smoked and has no history of asthma or allergies. Physical examination reveals bilateral inspiratory crackles. She appears unwell and is using accessory muscles of respiration.

vital_signs.oxygen_saturation: 89% on room air, 95% on 4L nasal prongs
vital_signs.peak_flow: Unable to perform due to dyspnoea

physical_examination.general_appearance: Acutely unwell, flushed, dyspnoeic, using accessory muscles
physical_examination.hands: No clubbing, mild peripheral cyanosis, farmer's hands with callouses
physical_examination.cardiovascular: Tachycardic, regular rhythm, no murmurs, JVP not elevated
physical_examination.respiratory: Tachypnoeic, bilateral fine inspiratory crackles throughout all lung fields, no wheeze, no pleural rub
physical_examination.neurological: Alert and oriented, no focal deficits

blood_tests.FBC: Hb 138 g/L, WCC 14.2 x 10^9/L (neutrophils 11.8, lymphocytes 1.2, eosinophils 0.2), platelets 342 x 10^9/L
blood_tests.biochemistry: Na 138 mmol/L, K 3.9 mmol/L, Cr 68 μmol/L, eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73m²
blood_tests.LFT: ALT 42 U/L, AST 48 U/L, ALP 92 U/L, LDH 428 U/L (elevated)
blood_tests.abg_on_4L: pH 7.46, PaO2 76 mmHg, PaCO2 32 mmHg, HCO3 22 mmol/L, SaO2 95%

imaging.chest_xray: Bilateral diffuse ground-glass opacities, no consolidation, no pleural effusion
imaging.hrct_chest: Widespread ground-glass opacification, centrilobular nodules, mosaic attenuation pattern, no honeycombing

immunology.precipitins: Pending - Thermophilic actinomycetes, Aspergillus fumigatus, bird proteins

immediate: Supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs 4-6L/min to maintain SpO2 >92%
Prednisolone 50 mg oral daily (PBS code 2089W)
Continuous pulse oximetry monitoring
Strict avoidance of hay and mouldy organic material
IV access and fluid resuscitation if dehydrated
investigations: Serum precipitins to thermophilic actinomycetes and moulds
Specific IgG antibodies to farmer's lung antigens
Bronchoscopy with BAL showing lymphocytosis (CD4/CD8 ratio)
Pulmonary function tests when acute phase resolved
Echocardiogram if concerns about pulmonary hypertension
Environmental sampling of hay for fungal culture
definitive: Continue prednisolone 50 mg daily for 2 weeks then taper over 2-3 months
Environmental modification - avoid mouldy hay exposure
Use of N95/P2 respirator when handling hay mandatory
Consider automated feeding systems to reduce exposure
Hay storage improvement - ensure proper drying before storage
Regular lung function monitoring
prevention: Education about proper hay storage and moisture control
Implementation of mechanical ventilation in hay sheds
Use of sealed cabin tractors for hay handling
Regular use of appropriate respiratory protection (P2/N95 minimum)
Consider silage instead of hay where feasible
Workplace health and safety assessment by agricultural specialist
monitoring: Spirometry and DLCO at 4 weeks and 3 months
Monitor for progression to chronic/fibrotic HP
Annual surveillance spirometry if continuing farm work
Screen family members working with same exposure

communication_tasks: Explain hypersensitivity pneumonitis and triggering factors
Emphasise critical importance of exposure avoidance
Discuss need for workplace modifications on farm
Address concerns about ability to continue farming
Provide written action plan for symptom recurrence
Educate about proper use of respiratory protection
Discuss financial implications of workplace changes
Involve occupational hygienist for farm assessment

scoring_criteria.criterion: Recognises acute hypersensitivity pneumonitis from temporal relationship to exposure
Initiates corticosteroid therapy promptly
Orders specific precipitins and IgG antibodies for farmer's lung
Emphasises strict exposure avoidance as primary treatment
Provides appropriate oxygen therapy to correct hypoxaemia
Plans environmental assessment and modification of farm practices
Arranges appropriate follow-up with spirometry monitoring
Educates about respiratory protection and safe work practices
Addresses practical concerns about continuing farming occupation
Considers screening of other farm workers/family members
Documents detailed exposure history and temporal patterns

key_learning_points: Acute HP presents 4-8 hours after exposure with fever, dyspnoea, and crackles
Temporal relationship to exposure is key diagnostic feature
Serum precipitins positive in 50-70% but absence doesn't exclude diagnosis
Corticosteroids hasten recovery but avoidance is definitive treatment
Can progress to chronic fibrotic disease with continued exposure
Farmers often reluctant to change practices due to economic pressures
BAL lymphocytosis with low CD4/CD8 ratio supports diagnosis
red_flags: Severe hypoxaemia requiring high-flow oxygen or NIV
Failure to improve within 48-72 hours of steroid therapy
Signs of chronic fibrotic disease on imaging

title: Bronchiolitis Obliterans Syndrome - Post Lung Transplant
scenario: Robert Fleming, a 58-year-old retired teacher from Wahroonga, NSW, presents to the lung transplant clinic at St Vincent's Hospital 18 months after bilateral lung transplantation for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. He reports 2 months of progressive dyspnoea, now breathless walking 50 metres on flat ground. His FEV1 has declined from 3.2L (85% predicted) 6 months ago to 2.3L (61% predicted) currently. He has been adherent to his immunosuppression regimen and denies fever, cough, or sputum production. He lives with his wife and has been unable to return to his volunteer tutoring work. Recent surveillance bronchoscopy showed no acute rejection, and BAL was negative for infection.

vital_signs.oxygen_saturation: 92% on room air, 88% with minimal exertion

physical_examination.general_appearance: Well-groomed, cushingoid features from steroids, dyspnoeic with minimal exertion
physical_examination.hands: No clubbing, mild tremor (tacrolimus), no cyanosis
physical_examination.cardiovascular: Regular rhythm, no murmurs, mild ankle oedema bilaterally
physical_examination.respiratory: Bilateral thoracotomy scars well-healed, reduced chest expansion, scattered expiratory wheeze, no crackles
physical_examination.abdomen: Soft, central obesity, no tenderness, no organomegaly
physical_examination.neurological: Alert, oriented, fine tremor, no focal deficits
physical_examination.skin: Thin skin with easy bruising, purple striae on abdomen

blood_tests.FBC: Hb 112 g/L, WCC 8.2 x 10^9/L, platelets 186 x 10^9/L
blood_tests.biochemistry: Na 139 mmol/L, K 4.8 mmol/L, Cr 142 μmol/L (baseline 110), eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73m²
blood_tests.LFT: ALT 38 U/L, AST 42 U/L, ALP 98 U/L, bilirubin 18 μmol/L

imaging.chest_xray: Clear lung fields, no infiltrates, no pleural effusion
imaging.hrct_chest: Mosaic attenuation pattern, air trapping on expiratory images, bronchial wall thickening, no ground-glass changes

respiratory_function.spirometry: FEV1 2.3L (61% predicted) - decline from 3.2L, FVC 3.8L (78% predicted), FEV1/FVC 60%

bronchoscopy.transbronchial_biopsy: Grade A0 (no acute rejection), no infection
bronchoscopy.cultures: No bacterial, fungal, or mycobacterial growth

expected_diagnoses.primary: Bronchiolitis Obliterans Syndrome (BOS) - Chronic lung allograft dysfunction

immediate: Increase prednisolone to 30 mg daily for 2 weeks (PBS code 1646G)
Optimise tacrolimus level to 8-10 ng/mL
Add azithromycin 250 mg MWF (PBS code 8523T) - anti-inflammatory effect
Supplemental oxygen assessment and prescription if indicated
Pulmonary rehabilitation referral
investigations: Donor-specific antibody (DSA) testing
High-resolution CT chest in 4 weeks to assess progression
Repeat bronchoscopy with BAL for neutrophilia assessment
Gastro-oesophageal reflux assessment (24-hour pH study)
Fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) measurement
Consider lung biopsy if diagnosis uncertain
definitive: Consider switch from mycophenolate to everolimus 1 mg BD (PBS code 9431M)
Add montelukast 10 mg nocte (PBS code 8230J) for anti-inflammatory effect
Extracorporeal photopheresis if available and severe
Total lymphoid irradiation for refractory cases
Anti-reflux surgery if significant GORD identified
Re-transplantation evaluation if progressive despite treatment
supportive: Nutritional support to prevent further weight loss
monitoring: Monthly spirometry for first 3 months then 3-monthly
Skin cancer surveillance (increased risk with immunosuppression)

communication_tasks: Explain BOS diagnosis and chronic nature sensitively
Discuss prognosis (median survival 3-5 years after diagnosis)
Address treatment options including potential for re-transplantation
Explain importance of adherence to immunosuppression
Discuss infection prevention strategies
Involve spouse in care planning and support
Provide Lung Foundation Australia transplant resources
Discuss advance care directives and goals of care

scoring_criteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses BOS based on spirometry decline and exclusion of other causes
Excludes acute rejection and infection through appropriate investigations
Optimises immunosuppression appropriately
Initiates azithromycin for anti-inflammatory effect
Screens for gastro-oesophageal reflux as contributor
Refers for pulmonary rehabilitation
Addresses psychological impact and quality of life
Discusses prognosis honestly but sensitively
Plans appropriate surveillance and monitoring
Considers re-transplantation evaluation if appropriate
Involves multidisciplinary team appropriately

key_learning_points: BOS affects 50% of lung transplant recipients by 5 years
Defined as FEV1 decline >20% from baseline without other cause
Azithromycin has anti-inflammatory effects independent of antimicrobial action
GORD is important risk factor and should be aggressively treated
Median survival after BOS diagnosis is 3-5 years
Re-transplantation possible but outcomes generally poorer
Extracorporeal photopheresis may stabilise lung function in some cases
red_flags: New infiltrates suggesting infection or acute rejection

title: Cor Pulmonale Secondary to Severe COPD
scenario: Bruce Campbell, a 72-year-old retired coal miner from Cessnock, NSW, presents to the emergency department with worsening dyspnoea and bilateral leg swelling over 2 weeks. He has a 40-year history of underground coal mining and 50 pack-year smoking history (quit 5 years ago). He has severe COPD with multiple admissions in the past year and is on home oxygen 2L/min for 16 hours daily. His wife reports he has been increasingly drowsy and confused over the past 3 days. He currently takes tiotropium, budesonide/formoterol, and salbutamol. Examination reveals elevated JVP, bilateral pitting oedema to knees, and a loud P2 on auscultation.

physical_examination.general_appearance: Elderly man, drowsy but rousable, cyanosed lips and nail beds, using accessory muscles
physical_examination.hands: Clubbing present, nicotine staining, peripheral cyanosis, warm peripheries, bounding pulse
physical_examination.cardiovascular: JVP elevated to angle of jaw, irregular rhythm, loud P2, tricuspid regurgitation murmur, hepatojugular reflux positive
physical_examination.respiratory: Barrel chest, reduced expansion bilaterally, hyperresonant percussion, distant breath sounds, scattered wheeze, no crackles
physical_examination.abdomen: Distended, tender hepatomegaly 4 cm below costal margin, shifting dullness positive suggesting ascites
physical_examination.lower_limbs: Bilateral pitting oedema to knees, sacral oedema present
physical_examination.neurological: Drowsy but oriented to person only, asterixis present, no focal deficits

blood_tests.FBC: Hb 182 g/L (polycythaemia), WCC 9.2 x 10^9/L, platelets 156 x 10^9/L
blood_tests.biochemistry: Na 134 mmol/L, K 3.2 mmol/L, Cr 156 μmol/L (baseline 98), eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73m²
blood_tests.LFT: ALT 68 U/L, AST 72 U/L, ALP 142 U/L, albumin 28 g/L, INR 1.4

imaging.chest_xray: Hyperinflated lungs, flattened diaphragms, enlarged pulmonary arteries, cardiomegaly with prominent right heart border
imaging.ecg: Atrial fibrillation rate 102, right axis deviation, P pulmonale, incomplete RBBB, right ventricular strain pattern

echocardiogram.lv_function: Normal LV size and systolic function, EF 55%

expected_diagnoses.primary: Acute on chronic cor pulmonale secondary to severe COPD with hypercapnic respiratory failure

immediate: Controlled oxygen therapy 28% Venturi mask (target SpO2 88-92%)
BiPAP ventilation if no improvement (IPAP 14, EPAP 6, FiO2 28%)
Frusemide 40 mg IV stat then 40 mg oral BD (PBS code 2039Q)
Spironolactone 25 mg daily (PBS code 1790N) - potassium-sparing
Prednisolone 40 mg oral daily for 5 days (PBS code 2089W)
Continue tiotropium 18 mcg daily (PBS code 8562P)
Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg QID (PBS code 1819D)
investigations: CTPA to exclude pulmonary embolism
Right heart catheterisation for accurate PA pressures
Sleep study when stable to assess for OSA overlap
Spirometry and DLCO when stable
Coal workers' pneumoconiosis assessment
NT-proBNP trending
definitive: Long-term oxygen therapy review - increase to 24 hours daily
Consider sildenafil 20 mg TDS (PBS code 10208H) for pulmonary hypertension
Digoxin 125 mcg daily for rate control of AF (PBS code 2074T)
Anticoagulation with rivaroxaban 20 mg daily for AF (PBS code 10034K)
Pulmonary rehabilitation program when stable
Consider lung volume reduction surgery assessment
monitoring: Continuous pulse oximetry and capnography if available
Serial ABGs to monitor CO2 retention
Renal function and electrolytes daily while on diuretics
INR monitoring if commenced on warfarin
long_term: Home BiPAP if hypercapnic respiratory failure persists
Advance care planning and resuscitation discussion
Palliative care referral for symptom management
Coal Mine Workers' Compensation claim assessment

communication_tasks: Explain cor pulmonale as right heart strain from lung disease
Discuss poor prognosis (50% 2-year mortality)
Address goals of care and ceiling of treatment
Explain importance of oxygen therapy compliance
Educate about fluid restriction and daily weights
Involve family in advance care planning discussions
Provide COPD Foundation resources
Discuss eligibility for coal workers' compensation

scoring_criteria.criterion: Recognises cor pulmonale from clinical and echo findings
Manages hypercapnic respiratory failure with controlled oxygen
Initiates appropriate diuresis for right heart failure
Considers BiPAP for hypercapnic respiratory failure
Addresses atrial fibrillation with rate control and anticoagulation
Excludes pulmonary embolism as precipitant
Optimises COPD therapy including steroids for exacerbation
Addresses polycythaemia and considers venesection
Initiates advance care planning discussion
Considers occupational lung disease compensation
Plans appropriate long-term oxygen therapy

key_learning_points: Cor pulmonale is right heart failure secondary to lung disease
Controlled oxygen therapy crucial - target SpO2 88-92% in CO2 retainers
BiPAP reduces mortality in hypercapnic respiratory failure
Diuretics improve symptoms but don't alter prognosis
50% mortality within 2 years of cor pulmonale diagnosis
Coal workers may be eligible for dust diseases compensation
Polycythaemia secondary to chronic hypoxia increases thrombosis risk
red_flags: Altered mental status from CO2 narcosis
Acute kidney injury from cardiorenal syndrome
